Title: Cardiovascular Events Following Cancer Therapy in a Patient with Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
PMID: 
Authors: 

Abstract
Lung cancer is among the most diagnosed cancers worldwide, and its co-occurrence with coronary heart disease is life-threatening. Osimertinib is the standard treatment for epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations in advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The addition of pemetrexed and carboplatin increases not only the efficacy but also the cardiotoxicity risk. We report a 59-year-old woman with NSCLC alongside brain, liver, and spleen metastases, who developed cardiovascular events following cancer therapy. With advanced imaging and multidisciplinary intervention, remarkable remission was achieved over two years. Reporting this case contributes to the understanding of its presentation and diagnostic challenges.

2. Case presentation
A 59-year-old Saudi woman with a known history of asthma, hypertension, diabetes, and significant shisha (waterpipe) smoking presented to our hospital with a main complaint of coughing up yellowish thick sputum and unintentional weight loss of approximately 2 kg over the past three weeks. Her vitals were stable except for mild hypertension (131/73 mmHg). Physical examination revealed diminished left upper lung sounds without respiratory distress.
Chest computed tomography (CT) (Fig. 1) identified a 7 × 5 cm mass in the upper lobe of the left lung. Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) detected a primary hypermetabolic left upper lung mass with metastases to the brain, liver, and spleen (Fig. 2A). Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed multiple supratentorial and dural-based enhancing lesions. A CT-guided biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of a poorly differentiated NSCLC of epithelial origin, trefoil factor 1 (TFF1) positive with scattered P40+ cells, indicating adenosquamous carcinoma subtype, positive for EGFR exon 19 deletion (p. E746_T751del).
After diagnosis, the patient underwent a combination of chemotherapy and radiation therapy targeting both the primary lung tumor and the metastases, as demonstrated in the chronological timeline (Table 1). The patient was started on palliative whole brain radiation therapy (WBRT) to manage the metastatic lesions. Later, WBRT was discontinued, and she was started on osimertinib 80 mg/day for four months (day 24). Unexpectedly, a mixed therapeutic response was observed because liver metastasis showed progressive changes. A subsequent ultrasound-guided needle core liver biopsy confirmed metastatic adenocarcinoma of lung origin with no liver cirrhosis. In September 2022 (day 157), therapy was switched to carboplatin and reduced-dose pemetrexed for six cycles over four months. Maintenance with pemetrexed and osimertinib followed. After two years of this complex treatment, a PET/CT scan in May 2024 showed a significant reduction in the size of the primary lung tumor and regression of the metastases (Fig. 2B).
One month later, she developed acute dyspnea secondary to pulmonary edema and was treated with IV diuretics elsewhere. In June 2024 (day 779), she presented to our hospital and was seen by cardiology specialists for further evaluation. Her blood tests were remarkable for elevated brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) at 44.7 pmol/L and N-terminal proBNP (NT-proBNP) at 266.7 pmol/L, with normal troponin I levels. Based on all the previous findings, a cardiac PET/CT scan was performed and severe myocardial ischemia in the inferior and lateral walls was confirmed. Diagnostic catheterization was performed and showed a critical occlusion in the left anterior descending (LAD) artery with diagonal lesions (Fig. 3A). Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) was delayed until oncology clearance permitted dual antiplatelet therapy, after which successful stenting was performed (day 808) (Fig. 3B).
She was discharged in stable condition. At the last follow-up, therapy adherence was suboptimal owing to renal concerns; pemetrexed dose was adjusted. PET/CT showed benign post-treatment inflammation (Hopkins score 3). Repeat imaging was scheduled after four months.
